items.title: Buddy DeFranco interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 13, 1996
items.q: And Dizzy spelled it out pretty well

ctx.x: I mean the music you were playing, it was so connected with black culture and there you were in the middle of it.

That’s right. And half, maybe more than half of jazz, was created by white people. And Dizzy spelled it out pretty well, we had — utilizing African and Latin rhythms and Caucasian and Asian harmonies, and put that together and play jazz. So that was you know a conscious effort to work together, and it worked. So there was no room for a differences of races. Once in a while you might experience that in the music business but rarely, rarely in the jazz field, in those days. It changed you know. But in those days it…
So shortly after that group, Basie was able to, economically I guess, add his people back.

items.title: DeFranco Buddy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: And Bird was there, and Dizzy.

ctx.x: Well I’m looking at your third Metronome All-Stars session in ’48 – ’49.
And Bird was there, and Dizzy.
And it’s Bird, and Dizzy, and Miles, and J.J. Johnson, Lennie Tristano, among others. It’s just an amazing line up.
